  Research Interests & Approach
  How I think about cities
  
    My research sits at the intersection of urbanism, landscape architecture, and spatial data science — with urban resilience and climate adaptation as the central thread. I am drawn to questions about how cities respond to pressure, where they fail, and what kinds of spatial interventions actually make a measurable difference.
    I work predominantly with quantitative methods — GIS, QGIS, R — applying spatial analysis and modeling to understand urban systems and assess the performance of design and planning solutions. What drives me is the belief that better questions and better tools can lead to better cities.
    Lately I have been deeply curious about what artificial intelligence means for how we teach and practice spatial and urban design — not as a shortcut, but as a genuinely new way of engaging with complex spatial problems.
  
  
    ● Now · Active
    I am assembling a new research team and actively looking for collaborators — researchers, doctoral candidates, and practitioners who share a commitment to data-driven approaches to urban resilience. I am also seeking partnerships with municipalities and public organisations. → Get in touch
  




  
  




  Teaching & Community
  Building capacity, together
  
    I believe that methodological literacy is one of the most empowering things we can give to the next generation of urban professionals. At TU Delft, I coordinate the Spatial Data and GIS learning line in the MSc Urbanism programme — making rigorous spatial thinking accessible, reproducible, and genuinely useful for designers and planners.
    I am also a founding and core member of the Rbanism Community — an open initiative advancing the use of R in urbanism and spatial research. Building that community has reinforced something I care about deeply: sharing methods and knowledge across disciplines makes all of our work better.

title: Daniele Cannatella
text:
I am an urbanist fascinated by the question of how cities can become more resilient — and by the data, methods, and ideas we need to get there.
I work as an Assistant Professor in Urban Data for Design at TU Delft, in the Section of Urban Data Science within the Department of Urbanism, Faculty of Architecture and the Built Environment. My research sits at the crossroads of urbanism, landscape architecture, and spatial data science, and I approach urban problems through a quantitative lens — using GIS, QGIS, and R to analyze, model, and assess how cities respond to climate pressures and how interventions actually perform on the ground.
I am particularly interested in urban resilience and climate adaptation: not as abstract concepts, but as design and planning challenges that require rigorous spatial thinking, careful measurement, and a willingness to work across disciplinary boundaries.

title: Daniele Cannatella
text:
Teaching & Community
At TU Delft, I coordinate the Spatial Data and GIS learning line in the MSc Urbanism programme. I am also a founding and core member of the Rbanism Community, an open initiative advancing the use of R in urbanism and spatial research.
Lately, I have been exploring what artificial intelligence means for how we teach and practice spatial and urban design — and I find that question as exciting as it is open.

title: Daniele Cannatella
text:
What I’m Working On
I am currently setting up a new research team and actively looking for collaborators — researchers, students, and practitioners who share an interest in data-driven approaches to urban resilience and climate adaptation. I am also building partnerships with municipalities and public organizations.
If any of this resonates, I’d love to hear from you.

Research Themes



🌊 Urban Resilience
Assessing and modeling how urban systems withstand and recover from climate-related pressures.


🌿 Climate Adaptation
Evaluating the spatial performance and impact of green and blue infrastructure interventions.


🗺️ Spatial Data Science
Developing and applying GIS, R-based workflows, and computational methods for urban analysis.

title: Teaching
text: I believe that methodological literacy is one of the most empowering things we can give to the next generation of urban professionals. My teaching connects spatial data science with design thinking — helping students ask better questions, work with real data, and build rigorous, reproducible workflows.

title: Teaching
text:
Teaching Philosophy
I approach teaching as an act of translation: between disciplines, between methods, and between data and design. I want students to leave my courses not just knowing how to run an analysis, but understanding why it matters and how to communicate what they find.
I am also actively exploring the role of artificial intelligence in spatial and urban design education — not as a shortcut, but as a genuinely new way of engaging with complex urban problems.
